title: Grace gives the Word
hookLine: the Word comes by grace, and with it the bliss (Anand)

lines: WE'RE USED TO KEEPING ACCOUNTS EVEN.
THE ANAND: IT ARRIVES LIKE THAT.
cards: You reach the front of the line at a coffee counter and the barista says: it's paid for. The person ahead of you covered it and left. No name, no way to pay them back.
For some, the first feeling is a small awkwardness. People are used to earning things, trading, keeping the account even. A gift with no way to return it is strangely hard to hold.
The Anand says the most important thing a person can receive arrives exactly like that.

teach.h: GUR PARSAADEE: BY THE GURU'S GRACE.
teach.b: Listen back over this week's pauris and one phrase keeps returning: gur parsaadee, by the Guru's grace. The body pauri said that by the Guru's grace the Lord comes to dwell in the mind.
The light pauri said that by the Guru's grace a person understands. The eyes pauri said: by the Guru's grace I understood that the Lord is one.

teach.h: IT RETURNS AT EVERY TURNING POINT.
teach.b: Again and again, at a pauri's turning point, it doesn't say by effort, or cleverness, or study. It says grace. Earlier, it said the same in other words: the gift is given to the one the Lord blesses.
The phrase is on the first page too. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, ends on it: gur prasaad, known by the Guru's grace.

teach.h: NADAR, KIRPA, KARAM: WORDS FOR GRACE.
teach.b: Gurbani uses several words for grace. Nadar is a glance, the look of the Lord resting on someone. Kirpa is mercy.
Karam, in gurbani, can mean grace, a gift freely given. And the grace here comes through the Guru: gur parsaadee, not a lucky break. So what does grace give?

teach.h: GRACE GIVES THE WORD; THE WORD, BLISS.
teach.b: In the Anand, it gives the Word, the Guru's shabad, and with the Word comes anand, bliss. That doesn't make effort pointless; Sikh life is full of discipline, work and service. It changes what the effort is for.
You don't buy the gift. You keep the door open, and say thank you.

how: Sikhs speak of grace as nadar, kirpa or gur prasaad, and the phrase gur prasaad closes the Mool Mantar that opens the Guru Granth Sahib; many Sikhs begin and end their daily prayers by asking for the Guru's grace.

o: the reward that comes from hard effort
a sweet offering shared out after prayers
by the Guru's grace, a gift not earned

games.q: words for grace — tap the pairs.

s: at its turning points the Anand credits cleverness and study
again and again it says: by the Guru's grace.
the Mool Mantar ends with the words gur prasaad
teaching grace means Sikhs consider effort pointless
Sikh life is full of discipline, work and service; grace changes what the effort is for.

games.q: the Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, ends by saying how the One is known. what does it say?
o: by long study of the scriptures.
gur prasaad: by the Guru's grace.
games.why: it ends on gur prasaad, and the Anand keeps returning to the same phrase: by the Guru's grace.

practice: Notice one thing being given to you right now, with no bill attached: the floor holding you up, air arriving at every breath, light to see by.
Don't calculate whether you deserved it or plan how to repay it; just receive it, the way you'd take a warm cup somebody handed you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, as thanks.

wordCard.voice: Gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace. This week in the Anand: ripe words, ears tuned for the true, the body, the light, the eyes, the ears, the breath, and under all of it, gur prasaad.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace; the last words of the Mool Mantar.

carryVoice: Your line: grace gives. Like the stranger at the counter, it doesn't sign its name. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ramkali M3, Anand (gur parsaadee in the body, light and eyes pauris), Ang 917–922
